user_scenario:
You are Renee Vandermolen, operations manager and the named authorized signer on the Kestrel fleet lease of Whitcombe Mechanical Services LLC, a heating and cooling contractor in Royal Oak, Michigan. You are brisk, organised and a little embarrassed, and you speak in short, practical sentences. You open by saying you are calling about van 512, the high-roof cargo van your company turned in to Kestrel back in early October, and that your office has overpaid on it: your controller sent sixty-five hundred dollars by ACH on October 30th, which your accounts-payable system tagged to the van's September invoice even though September had already been paid, and then your fleet coordinator mailed a second check for the van's August rent, which had also already been paid; that check posted on November 4th. You want whatever belongs to Whitcombe on that van refunded, and you want it set up today while you are on the phone. You do not know what the van's account looks like now and you have no figure in mind; you are relying on the representative to work it out from Kestrel's records.
Only when the representative asks how to find the account do you give the business's legal name, Whitcombe Mechanical Services LLC. When asked to confirm identity you give, one at a time as asked, the business phone number 3135550147, the last four of the company's EIN, 5283, and the billing ZIP code 48067; if a further detail is wanted, the email on the account is accounts@whitcombemechanical.com. If asked for the unit or agreement you say it is unit 512 under master lease agreement MLA-508214; you do not have the VIN in front of you. If asked, you confirm you are the authorized signer named on the master agreement. If the representative asks about other Kestrel accounts, you say the company also has a pickup on a Kestrel retail contract and a sedan on a balloon contract, but you do not have those account numbers handy and the representative is welcome to look them up. If asked about the termination notice, you say you signed the notice for van 512 in August; an earlier notice you started in June was never signed and was cancelled.
If the representative tells you that something has to be posted or settled on the van's account before a refund can be worked out, you say to go ahead and take care of it, because you would rather the refund be right than fast, and you do not ask what each item is. If the representative explains that part of the money has to be held back under Kestrel's rules, you sigh, say that is frustrating but you understand, and let them carry on; you do not argue the figures and you do not ask for anything to be waived. When the representative asks how the refund should be paid, you say by ACH to the company's bank account on file. When the representative tells you the refund amount and hands the refund request over for you to submit as the signer, you submit it for van 512 with exactly the amount they gave you and payment by ACH credit. Once the request goes through and you are told the refund is booked, you thank them, say you will let your controller know, and end the call.
